2. In Memobiam.�Hooper C. Van Vorst (0, '39), died in New York,
October 26th, 1889. An associate of the founders of the Fraternity, Judge
Van Vorst retained always a lively interest in its welfare and prosperity, and
his influence and efforts were ever at its service. At a memorial meeting at
the Psi Upsilon Club House in New York, November 12th, 1889, an appropri
ate minute, expressing the sense of loss sustained by the Fraternity in Judge
Van Vorst's death, was adopted, and a copy will be transmitted to the Convenr
tion. The Council adds its tribute to those which have already been recorded,,
and suggests that the Convention take suitable action.

4. Finances. �
The treasury of the Fraternity has been in excellent condition
during the year. The treasurer's statement is hereto annexed. The balance
on hand is $1475.32, consisting of cash and deposits in the Broadway Savings
Institution and the 4th National Bank, New York City. Of this sum $386.83 is
to the credit of the Convention Fund, and the remainder, $1088.49, is applic
able to the general uses of the Fraternity. It seems desirable that money should
be gradually provided for the publication of the new song book, so that there
may be enough on hand to pay for the work as it progresses, without the nee-

13
�essity, as in the case of the recent catalogue, of borrowing on individual credit
and imposing a burdensome assessment when the book is finally issued. For
this and other general purposes a tax of $1 per active member in 1891 is recom
mended.
Members of other fraternities have from time to time called the attention of
the members of the Council to the fact that a judgment for $269. 30 recovered
against the proprietor of The Diamond for printing that paper in 1885 and 1886
has been outstanding unpaid for several years. While it is quite true that The
Diamond was an individual enterprise, for which the Fraternity was not
responsible, and that its owner regards its debts as his personal affair, our
Fraternity name was so connected with the paper that we have plainly
incurred public discredit through its financial shortcomings. The matter has
been considered by former Conventions, and the Council was once authorized
to settle the claim, but the authority was withdrawn by the Convention of
1889, on Mr. Allison's personal statement of his own wishes. The failure to
dispose of the judgment still continues, however, and has been urged upon us
so
frequently that the members of the Council feel impelled to say that, in
their deliberate opinion, private considerations should now be outweighed by
regard for the reputation of the Fraternity. The recommendation is, therefore,
made that the Council shall be authorized to buy the judgment, so that it shall
not, while unpaid, be held in an
unfriendly iaterest.
5. The 10th Catalogue. �
One hundred and five catalogues have been dis
posed of during the year, realizing, chiefly through the payment of assessments,
$515.91.
The Xi paid its assessment prior to the Convention of 1889, but too late for
mention in the last Annual Communication. The Delta and Zeta have recently
"made their final payments with interest. The Iota, Psi and Eta are stiU in
arrears and report that they have been unable to pay because of serious diffi
culties arising from various local causes. The matter may well be considered
by the Convention with a view to some definite arrangement under which the
debt may be paid in regular annual installments.
Enough copies of the catalogue remain unsold to supply any reasonable
demand.

APPENDIX B.
Dickinson College,
Caelisle, Pa., April 19, 1890.
To the General Convention and the several Chapters of the Psi Upsilon
Fraternity :
Gentlemen, �
The undersigned members of the Junior, Sophomore, and Freshmen
Classes in Dickinson College respectfully petition you to establish at this Insti
tution a Chapter of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity .
The history, present condition and prospects of the College are such as to
warrant this appeal, as will be seen by the enclosed endorsement of President
Reed and Prof. Whiting, Members of the Fraternity.
Before entering college many of us had conceived a great admiration for
your Fraternity, and since our entrance, though importuned constantly and
earnestly, we have refrained from connecting ourselves with any other organi
zation with the view of this petition, and, encouraged by our President and
Professor above alluded to, we have formed and maintained our organization
hoping that our
request will be granted.
We can guarantee that the Chapter will at once take high rank both in the
college and in the community.
In addition to those already named there are local members, one of whom
Wm. Tricket, L.L.D., is an author eminent in the law.
Founded in 1783, Dickinson College has a
long line of distinguished
Alumni ; enrolled in its list are a President and a Chief Justice of the United
States, and many names great in church and state.
We pledge ourselves, should you accede to our
request, never to suUy the
fair name of your honored body, and to maintain the high standard that has
ever characterized Psi Upsilon.
We can assure you of securing a
permanent home in the near future.
Hoping for favorable action upon our
petition, we remain

The undersigned. Professors and Students of the University of Minne
sota, and members of Theta Phi local Fraternity, respectfully petition and
urge that Theta Phi be granted a Charter of PsiUpsilon, and that its members

It is now nearly ten years since we first asked for admission, and the pre
sent is our fifth petition ; but, although heretofore doomed to disappointment
we have never for a moment been discouraged or lost faith in our ultimate suc
cess. The University of Minnesota, with its central location in the Metropolis
of the Northwest, with its magnificent endowment, with its numerous build
ings and complete equipment, with its large and able corps of instructors, with
its large attendance, and supported by a
generous legislature, is easily the
greatest institution of learning in the Northwest. And in this University, not
withstanding many competitors, no Fraternity ranks higher than Theta Phi,

been leaders in University affairs assure Psi Upsilon of a strong and energetic
Chapter from the very Start. Unlike the experience of most newly estabhshed
Chapters the Theta Phi Chapter'] of Psi Upsilon would from the first take a
